newsitem.title: USA: Clinton well up in Pennsylvania, New Jersey - poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton well up in Pennsylvania, New Jersey - poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton leads Republican Bob Dole by 15.4 percentage points in a Reuters poll of voter sentiment across the neighbouring battleground states of Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

The poll of 997 likely voters, conducted Sept 22-24 by John Zogby Group International, gave Clinton an aggregate of 47.6 percent in the two states. Dole had 32.2 percent and Reform Party candidate Ross Perot had 6.5 percent. Some 12.8 percent of respondents were undecided. The poll carried a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.

Clinton's lead was slightly greater in Pennsylvania, where he led Dole by 16 percentage points. In New Jersey, Dole was 14.6 points behind. The margin of error for the Pennsylvania sub-group was plus or minus four percentage points. For New Jersey, it was plus or minus five points.

The poll was yet another sign that Clinton remains comfortably positioned to triumph in the Nov. 5 election. Both states have popular Republican governors and swung heavily Republican in the 1994 congressional elections.
Both candidates have campaigned heavily in both states. Clinton was in New Jersey Tuesday and Pennsylvania Wednesday.
Pollster John Zogby noted that in this poll, as in all previous Reuters polls, Dole's support remained mired well below 40 percent.
"Dole appears hopelessly locked in the 30's nationally and state by state. At some point Dole will have to move up into the 40s if he is to make this a race," said Zogby.
With 270 Electoral College votes needed to win the presidency in the indirect U.S. system, Pennsylvania is the fifth biggest state with 23 votes. New Jersey has 15 votes.
A Reuters poll last week found Clinton with similar leads in the Midwestern states of Michigan, Ohio and Illinois, which have a combined 61 Electoral College votes.
The poll came at the end of a week when Dole repeatedly blamed Clinton in speeches and paid advertisements for an increase in the use of illegal drugs by young people.
But a large majority of voters said they disagreed that Clinton was responsible. In both states, only 20 percent said they agreed with Dole's argument, while 70 percent disagreed.

Dole's other top issue, his promise of a 15 percent income tax cut, was modelled on the strategy that helped New Jersey Gov. Christine Todd Whitman score a come-from-behind victory over Democrat Jim Florio to win the governorship in 1993.
But in follow-up interviews voters, including many Republicans and Dole supporters, continued to express deep scepticism that Dole could deliver.

"I don't agree with Dole's tax cut. Somewhere down the road, we'll all have to pay for it," said Gary Clemons, a casket maker in Mount Wolf, Pennsylvania, who nevertheless said he would support the Republican nominee.
Others are not so charitable. The poll showed that only 62 percent of Republicans are backing Dole while 76 percent of Democrats support Clinton.
Several voters also criticised Dole for opposing Perot's inclusion in the upcoming presidential debates.

"Perot should be in the debates. It was misguided of Dole to oppose him. He's listening to his advisers who have him convinced he's an old man who knows nothing about politics, which is ludicrous," said Diane McClarty, a homemaker from Montclair, New Jersey who backed Perot in 1992 but supports Dole this time.
The poll showed a continued wide gender gap. Clinton led by only eight points among men but by 23 points among women.

"Republican policies have become very mean-spirited. Women care more about education, children and the underprivileged and these issues are the heart of this election," said Deborah Hill-Haney, a chemist from Metuchen, New Jersey.
In congressional races. Democrats had small leads in both states -- five points in Pennsylvania and less than one point in New Jersey.
Clinton carried New Jersey by just over two percentage points in 1992 and Pennsylvania by nine points.
